newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: National won't cut off NZ First - Bolger.
newsitem.headline: National won't cut off NZ First - Bolger.

text.p: New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger on Monday acknowledged his National Party was being damaged by the controversy surrounding coalition partner New Zealand First, but he said without NZ First National would be in opposition.
Bolger, speaking after the National Party conference at the weekend, dismissed criticism of New Zealand First.
"I'm thanking them and so did the conference in its own way -- otherwise we would be in opposition," he told Radio New Zealand.
"If the NZ First decision had been to go with Labour and the Alliance, we would have been up there yesterday moaning about the opposition, moaning about the country going to the left."

Bolger also made a veiled criticism of Maori Affairs Minister and NZ First deputy leader Tau Henare, who was alleged at the weekend to have threatened TV3's funding after an altercation with a TV3 journalist.
"I don't think anybody should be threatening anybody. We've got a privileges case on where alleged threats were made as well. So yes, some of these issues are untidy."
The privileges committee is due to rule on allegations that NZ First leader Winston Peters breached parliamentary privilege by assaulting National backbencher John Banks.
Bolger said National would not cut NZ First off.
"We happen to have a very small majority between the National Party-NZ First coalition, and you just don't have the luxury of cutting this one off or that one off."
He said there was no doubt National would be hurt in the polls because of the scandal surrounding NZ First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan.
"I think we'll suffer in the opinion polls for a while. There is a public perception that this hasn't been good in terms of the sideshows of politics."
Bolger said it was not his role to take action against individual MPs who had been elected to parliament, although he continually received letters from the public asking him to.

"The public is always wanting me to straighten up someone or other. My dilemma is simple. I don't select members of parliament at all. They are elected by the public, they are sent to Wellington to do a job. I work with them as best I can in a team approach when they are on my side of the House."
Bolger repeated that he was confident he would lead the National Party into the next election, dismissing speculation of leadership bids next year.
